analysis.one_liner: Makes price gouging during emergencies a federal offense enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved since July 17, 2025, when it was introduced by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with 9 Democratic and independent cosponsors and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal violation to charge a "grossly excessive price" for any good or service, with the tightest rules kicking in during emergencies — disasters, power outages, pandemics, or sudden trade shocks. Large companies (those with over $1 billion in US revenue) would be presumed to be price gouging if they charged more during an emergency than before it, unless they could prove the increase came from costs beyond their control. The Federal Trade Commission could sue violators directly in court and impose penalties up to 5 percent of a parent company's revenue, state attorneys general could sue too, and public companies would have to disclose in SEC filings how much of their revenue growth came from raising prices rather than selling more. Small businesses under $100 million in revenue would be exempt if their price increases reflected costs they couldn't control.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially during emergencies. When hurricanes knock out power, pandemics disrupt supply chains, or disasters hit, prices for essentials like food, fuel, generators, and lodging can multiply. Today, price-gouging rules exist only at the state level and vary widely in what they cover and when. This bill would create a nationwide standard enforced by the FTC, allow restitution for cheated consumers, and let every state attorney general sue in federal court. It also targets the whole supply chain, so wholesalers and distributors — not just retail clerks — could be held accountable for jacking up prices mid-chain.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for anyone in a supply chain to sell a good or service at a 'grossly excessive price,' not just retailers at the final sale [S2].

During an 'exceptional market shock' — a disaster, power failure, public health emergency, trade-policy shift, or other atypical disruption — a large company that raises prices well above its own pre-shock prices or competitors' prices is presumed to be violating the law unless it can show the increase came from costs outside its control [S2].

The FTC can go directly to federal court to stop violations, win restitution and damages for consumers, and impose civil penalties; companies with over $1 billion in US revenue face penalties up to 5 percent of their parent company's revenue [S2].

State attorneys general can bring their own enforcement actions in federal or state court and recover compensation for their residents, and nothing in the bill overrides stronger state price-gouging laws [S2].

Public companies must disclose, in SEC filings covering any quarter with an exceptional market shock, how much of their revenue growth came from higher prices versus higher volume, their gross margins by product line, and a narrative explanation of their pricing decisions — making it easier to see when price increases outpaced costs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their shareholders. Companies with over $1 billion in US revenue would face a legal presumption that emergency price increases are gouging, civil penalties up to 5 percent of their total revenue per violation, and new public disclosure of their pricing strategies and margins in SEC filings. The bill is funded by a $1 billion appropriation to the FTC, which comes from the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the FTC to define key terms by rule — what counts as a 'grossly excessive price,' what counts as a market, and what counts as an exceptional market shock — so the real reach of the ban would depend on how the Commission writes those rules, creating uncertainty for businesses that must price goods under emergency conditions [S2].

During an exceptional market shock, large companies are presumed to be violating the law if they charge more than before the shock, and they must rebut that presumption with clear and convincing evidence that the increase came from costs outside their control — a heavy burden that could discourage legitimate price increases when supply costs genuinely rise [S2].

Penalties for companies with unfair leverage can reach 5 percent of the ultimate parent entity's total annual revenue, a very large exposure that is calculated on company-wide revenue rather than the revenue tied to the violation [S2].

Public companies would face new detailed SEC disclosure obligations during any quarter with an exceptional market shock — including gross margins by product category and a narrative explaining their pricing decisions — adding compliance costs that are ultimately passed through to consumers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: prices for essentials can spike during emergencies, and most states have only patchy price-gouging laws that cover limited goods and time windows, while this would apply nationwide to any good or service [S2]. The main costs are on the business side: the "grossly excessive price" standard is left largely to FTC rulemaking, penalties can reach 5 percent of a parent company's total revenue, and large firms would face a legal presumption against them during emergencies that they must overcome with clear and convincing evidence [S2]. Honest supporters would acknowledge that a broad federal standard enforced by penalties of that size could make companies overly cautious about raising prices even when their own costs genuinely rise, and that the $1 billion appropriation is a large sum for a new enforcement program [S2]. Weighing this honestly, the bill's consumer benefit is large and its compliance costs fall on companies with the revenue to absorb them, but the breadth of the standard and the reliance on FTC rulemaking mean the practical line between gouging and legitimate pricing would depend heavily on how the Commission writes its rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote ever since; with Congress still in session, it could still move, but no action has been taken.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history is two entries: it was introduced in the Senate on July 17, 2025, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S4].
Since then, the committee has taken no action — no hearings, no markup, no vote have been scheduled or recorded [S1].
It has 9 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one independent, with no Republican support on the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything concrete, because the bill has not advanced beyond its committee referral. If it stays stalled, large corporations that would face federal price-gouging penalties and new pricing disclosures are better off, since the restrictions never take effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; large firms benefit if it stalls

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set its terms: a federal price-gouging ban with FTC enforcement, penalties scaled to company revenue, and new SEC pricing disclosures.

for.name: Sens. Baldwin, Blumenthal, Fetterman, Kim, Markey, Merkley, Sanders, Slotkin, and Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill its full current roster of 10 supporters.

for.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 17, 2025, and has taken no recorded action on it since — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican has joined, and no member of either party has voted on the bill.

industries.industry: Large retailers, grocers, and consumer goods companies
industries.note: Companies with over $1 billion in US revenue would face a federal ban on grossly excessive prices, a presumption of violation during emergencies that they must rebut with clear and convincing evidence, and civil penalties up to 5 percent of their parent company's revenue. These firms profit most from selling essentials at scale during shortages, so a binding federal price cap cuts directly against that.

Any public company would have to disclose in SEC filings, during quarters with an exceptional market shock, how much revenue growth came from price versus volume, its gross margins by product line, and its pricing rationale. This is a compliance cost for the companies but a transparency gain for consumers and investors.

industries.industry: Small businesses (under $100 million in parent revenue)
industries.note: Firms whose ultimate parent earned under $100 million in US revenue in the prior year are exempt from the ban if their price increases reflect costs beyond their control. The bill's restrictions effectively target large corporations rather than small merchants.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing or markup usually die quietly at the end of a Congress, and this one has no Republican cosponsors, so it is unlikely to reach the Senate floor unless it is attached to a larger moving vehicle. Its most realistic paths are sitting in committee until the 119th Congress ends, or parts of it reappearing in a broader consumer-protection or emergency-pricing package.
